title: Designing Confidentiality into Quantum Encrypted Cloning: Which Subsets Leak, How Much, and When None Do
content: Quantum encrypted cloning introduces redundancy into quantum storage without violating the no- cloning theorem: an unknown state is encoded into several signal-key pairs, and only authorized subsets can recover it. Lack of authorization, however, is not the same as confidentiality, since an unauthorized subset need not be completely uninformative. This paper analyses its confidentiality. We classify the subsets of the encoded system as fully informative, partially informative or completely uninformative, for qubits, and extend the classification to arbitrary finite dimension for the subsets that contain the input register, the case left open by the qudit literature. Three results then describe the residual leakage. It is delocalized: what leaks is shared among the n custodians of a leaking subset as an n-out-of-n threshold secret, so no proper coalition learns anything. It is bounded: never more than log2d bits in dimension d, and a single classical bit for qubits; what escapes is the statistics of one generalized Pauli observable, never the stored state. And it is avoidable: leakage is absent from every subset exactly when an arithmetic condition on the clone multiplicity holds, one that depends only on the prime factors of d and leaves about half the multiplicities available. On imperfect hardware, local noise on the stored registers can never create leakage, and neither can unital noise on the entangled resources. Independent coherent errors inside the encoding circuit are the harmful case: the leakage they create grows linearly with the error angle, is not attenuated by a larger multiplicity and, unlike in the ideal protocol, can be read by a single custodian. The encoding circuit, not the storage, is where confidentiality is decided. Clone multiplicity is thus a confidentiality parameter as well as a redundancy parameter.
